newsitem.title: GERMANY: Intel unveils cost-cutting PC design.
newsitem.headline: Intel unveils cost-cutting PC design.

text.p: Scores of personal computer suppliers plan to offer new PCs next month that reduce the cost of managing corporate computer networks, chip maker Intel Corp said on Wednesday.
The new "NetPCs", based on a blueprint developed by the chip giant, would cut by 30 percent or more the thousands of dollars it costs to keep PCs in working order, Intel said at the CeBIT trade fair.

The machines, due from scores of PC suppliers over the next 90 days at prices beginning at about $1,000, include features that allow companies to update PCs automatically and dramtically reduce the time it takes to install new software, Intel said.

"The biggest cost a company has is not the actual cost of the PC, but maintenance -- updating software or installing new drives," Pat Gelsinger, Intel's chief of desktop products, told Reuters. "We believe NetPCs will be the PCs companies will buy from now on."
Companies often spend $10,000 or more annually to manage each PC in its network, according to industry consultant Forrester Research.
The NetPC design, which lets companies install software by sending updates out over the network, could shave thousands of dollars off the cost of maintaining a computer, Gelsinger said.
For large corporations, with thousands of PCs, the potential savings were substantial, he said.
In constrast to today's PCs, the NetPC design has a slimmed-down, sealed case and no general purpose slots for accessories -- to keep individual users from altering the settings on the systems.
The new machines also automatically recognise when they are connected to printers and can have their network connections set up from another computer in the next office or across the country.
Compaq Computer Corp., Dell Computer Corp. adn Hewlett Packard Co. helped Intel develop the NetPC design and would be among the first to launch machines that are "wired for management", Intel said.

"By the end of the second quarter we expect NetPCs to be shipping and available," Gelsinger said. The range of machines would include models with the 200 megaherz Pentium II chip Intel demonstrated at CeBIT ahead of its commercial release.
Later this year, Intel would offer similar cost-saving designs for portable PCs and servers, big machines that control networks.
Some of the features would find their way into home PCs in 1998, Gelsinger said. They could allow home users to log on to Internet sites for an on-line computer tune up, he said.
Intel hoped the management features would encourage companies to buy new PCs, Gelsinger said.
"If you reduce the cost of ownership, you remove a barrier to new PC purchases," he said.
